books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text: A black-and-white painting of Sutter's Mill on the American River at Coloma, California: a wooden mill building with a millrace in the foreground, small houses and trees around it, and hills rising behind.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The discovery at this mill most directly led to which of the following consequences for California?

options.text: California's Indian peoples gained new reservations with secure land titles from the state.
options.misconception: The rush devastated California's Indian peoples; their population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to under 30,000 by the Civil War.

options.text: Mexico regained California under the Gadsden Purchase of 1853.
options.misconception: The Gadsden Purchase added a strip south of the Gila; it did not return California to Mexico.

options.text: The United States banned all further migration to the West after the discovery.
options.misconception: Migration westward only grew after the discovery, as tens of thousands rushed to California.

options.text: California filled with settlers so fast that it applied for statehood within two years.

rationales.A: The gold rush brought disease, violence, and land loss to California Indians; their numbers collapsed, they gained no secure reservations.
rationales.B: The Gadsden Purchase of 1853 bought land south of the Gila River; California stayed American.
rationales.C: The rush sped migration west, it did not stop it; more than 80,000 came within a year.
rationales.D: The rush filled California so quickly that settlers wrote a constitution banning slavery in 1849 and the state entered the Union in 1850.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the crowd. Within a year of the discovery, more than 80,000 people poured into California.
2. Ask what a crowd that size needs: a government, laws, and a state.
3. See how fast it happened. Californians wrote a constitution in 1849 that banned slavery, and California entered the Union as a free state in 1850.
Remember: a gold strike can build a state overnight — and the state it built then forced the whole country to argue about slavery again.
